action: Cardiac-risk monitoring upgraded: 5-lead ECG with ST analysis, invasive arterial pressure considered, troponin available.
Avoid tachycardia: ketamine and pancuronium avoided; maintain heart rate close to baseline; treat tachycardia early with short-acting beta-blocker.
Avoid hypotension: induction agent dose reduced, vasopressor immediately available, MAP target maintained ≥ 70–75 mmHg.
Reduced left-ventricular function: titrated induction (etomidate / cautious propofol), avoid negative inotropes, inotrope support pre-prepared.
Antiplatelet therapy: continue aspirin perioperatively unless explicitly contraindicated; surgical bleeding risk discussed.
Anticoagulation: confirmed bridging plan (DOACs withheld 24–48 h, warfarin INR confirmed) and reversal agent identified.
Cardiac implantable device: pre-op interrogation confirmed, diathermy mode set to bipolar, magnet immediately available.
Pulmonary risk: lung-protective ventilation (Vt 6–8 mL/kg IBW, PEEP 5–8 cmH₂O), recruitment manoeuvres, post-op CPAP available.
Bronchospasm risk: salbutamol immediately available, deepen anaesthesia before instrumentation, consider regional/LMA in preference to ETT where appropriate.
OSA pathway: opioid-sparing technique prioritised, multimodal analgesia, extended PACU monitoring with continuous SpO₂; CPAP brought to recovery if home user.
Avoid prolonged high FiO₂: titrate to SpO₂ 92–96% to reduce risk of CO₂ retention.
Recent URI: elective procedures should be reconsidered; if proceeding, deep extubation, salbutamol pre-prepared, paediatric SAFE-T protocol applied.
Renal dose adjustment applied: avoid morphine and pethidine (active metabolites accumulate); prefer fentanyl/remifentanil; NSAIDs avoided.
Nephrotoxin avoidance: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and contrast minimised; isotonic crystalloid maintained; urine output monitored.
Potassium monitoring: pre-op K⁺ confirmed; avoid suxamethonium if K⁺ ≥ 5.0 mmol/L; ECG continuous monitoring for peaked T-waves.
Hepatic dose adjustment: induction agent dose reduced 30–50%; benzodiazepines minimised; cisatracurium preferred (organ-independent metabolism).
Coagulopathy: PT/INR and platelets confirmed pre-op; vitamin K / FFP / platelets prepared as indicated; neuraxial techniques re-evaluated.
Hepatotoxin avoidance: paracetamol dose-reduced, halothane avoided, sevoflurane preferred over isoflurane.
Glucose monitoring: capillary BG hourly intra-op; variable-rate insulin infusion if BG > 10 mmol/L; avoid lactated Ringer if hyperglycaemia significant.
Type 1 DM: long-acting insulin continued at reduced dose; short-acting omitted on day of surgery; ketones checked if BG > 14 mmol/L.
Steroid cover: hydrocortisone 50–100 mg IV at induction; supplementary doses for major surgery; usual daily dose continued post-op.
Thyroid storm risk: ensure euthyroid pre-op where elective; beta-blocker continued; avoid sympathetic stimulation; have hydrocortisone, propylthiouracil, propranolol available.
Phaeochromocytoma: confirmed alpha-blockade pre-op; arterial line pre-induction; phentolamine, magnesium, esmolol, GTN immediately available.
Airway risk identified: difficult-airway equipment immediately available (videolaryngoscope, bougie, supraglottic device range, surgical airway kit); pre-oxygenation extended.

Obesity weight basis: induction agents (propofol, thiopental) by lean body weight; muscle relaxants by ideal body weight; opioids generally by adjusted body weight; antibiotics by total body weight. Always titrate to clinical effect.
Sepsis pathway: surviving-sepsis bundle confirmed; lactate trended; balanced crystalloid resuscitation; noradrenaline first-line vasopressor.

Volume resuscitation needed: balanced crystalloid initial bolus (10–20 mL/kg) titrated to dynamic indices (PPV, lactate clearance, capillary refill) with frequent reassessment. Avoid fixed-volume protocols in patients at risk of fluid overload.
Full-stomach precautions: rapid-sequence induction, cricoid pressure considered, NG decompression where indicated, awake intubation if difficult airway co-exists.

Major trauma: damage control resuscitation, permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg until bleeding controlled, EXCEPT in TBI where MAP ≥ 80), 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets, tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 h (CRASH-2/3), warming.

Raised ICP / TBI: TIVA preferred (propofol + remifentanil), avoid ketamine and N₂O, head-up 15–30°, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40), MAP ≥ 80 (CPP > 60), avoid hypoxaemia, smooth induction/emergence to prevent ICP spikes.

Cervical-spine precautions / instability (e.g. rheumatoid atlantoaxial subluxation, Down syndrome): manual in-line stabilisation during intubation, videolaryngoscope first-line, awake fibreoptic if known significant instability, minimise neck movement, hard collar maintained until cleared. Consider flexion/extension imaging pre-op in high-risk groups.

Fixed/rigid cervical spine (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis, fused spine): anticipate difficult laryngoscopy from fixed flexion deformity — awake fibreoptic intubation is often the safest first choice, do NOT force the neck into "sniffing" position, prepare difficult-airway equipment, and note associated difficult neuraxial access and restrictive lung disease / aortic regurgitation.

Active haemorrhage: activate Major Haemorrhage Protocol (1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets), 2 large-bore IV access, rapid infuser, cell salvage if available, TXA 1 g IV (within 3 h), warming, point-of-care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) if available, fibrinogen ≥ 1.5 g/L (2 g/L in obstetric).

Acquired coagulopathy risk: baseline PT/APTT/fibrinogen + platelets, avoid neuraxial until corrected, prepare reversal if on anticoagulants (PCC for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors).

Active warming: forced-air warmer pre-induction and intra-op, fluid warmer, ambient theatre ≥ 21 °C, target core temperature ≥ 36 °C (NICE CG65). Hypothermia exacerbates coagulopathy and increases bleeding.
Pregnancy: aspiration prophylaxis (sodium citrate ± ranitidine), left lateral tilt 15°, avoid teratogens, foetal monitoring as appropriate to gestation.

Pre-eclampsia pathway: BP control + magnesium prophylaxis + careful fluid balance (≤ 80 mL/h to avoid pulmonary oedema) + document platelet count before any neuraxial. Avoid ergometrine and NSAIDs. See linked rules below for specific drug doses.

HELLP syndrome: critical obstetric emergency. Senior obstetric, anaesthetic and haematology input. Continuous foetal monitoring. Prepare for delivery — definitive treatment is delivery of the placenta. ICU/HDU bed required postpartum. Mild–moderate transaminitis common (AST/ALT 70–150 U/L typical) — titrate induction agents but routine 30–50% dose reduction usually unnecessary unless severe disease (Sibai class I) or coexisting hepatic failure.

Severe thrombocytopenia: full FBC with platelet count and trend within 6 h of any neuraxial decision. SOAP 2021 thresholds — spinal/epidural acceptable at platelets ≥ 70 × 10⁹/L if trend stable; 50–70 individualised with risk-benefit; < 50 contraindicated. ROTEM/TEG if available. Group and crossmatch 4 units; activate massive transfusion protocol if active bleeding.

Neuraxial / regional caution — bleeding or coagulation risk present: CHECK platelet count and coagulation (PT/APTT/fibrinogen, and a recent platelet trend) BEFORE any spinal, epidural or deep block. General guide — neuraxial acceptable at platelets ≥ 70–80 × 10⁹/L with normal coagulation and stable trend; 50–70 individualised (senior + haematology); < 50 generally contraindicated. Account for anticoagulant/antiplatelet timing (ASRA/AAGBI intervals). If neuraxial is contraindicated, plan a general anaesthetic and discuss alternatives. Spinal preferred over epidural where neuraxial is justified (smaller needle, lower haematoma volume).

Severe hypertension control (pre-eclampsia/HELLP): labetalol 10–20 mg IV (repeat q10 min, max 300 mg) OR hydralazine 5–10 mg IV (q15 min, max 30 mg) OR oral nifedipine 10 mg. Target BP 140–150 / 90–100 mmHg (do NOT drop precipitously — placental hypoperfusion). Continuous arterial line if labile or for delivery.

Magnesium sulphate seizure prophylaxis: 4 g IV loading over 5–10 min, then 1 g/h infusion for 24 h post-delivery (or 24 h after last seizure). Monitor for toxicity: deep tendon reflexes hourly; respiratory rate; serum Mg if oliguria or renal impairment. Antidote: calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly. Note: magnesium potentiates non-depolarising muscle relaxants — reduce dose 25–50%.

HELLP haemorrhage preparation: two large-bore IVs, group-and-save with 4 units crossmatched, fibrinogen and FFP available, cell salvage if accepted by patient. Anticipate PPH (uterine atony exacerbated by magnesium) and rare hepatic capsular haematoma/rupture. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV if PPH onset.

Perioperative anxiety: consider anxiolytic premedication (e.g. midazolam 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV titrated, or oral 7.5 mg ~30 min pre-op) balanced against day-case discharge and OSA/opioid sensitivity. Calm, unhurried environment; clear pre-op explanation; non-pharmacological measures (reassurance, parental presence in paediatrics). Avoid over-sedation in the elderly (delirium risk).

Chronic SSRI/SNRI therapy likely: avoid serotonergic combinations (pethidine, tramadol, methylene blue, high-dose ondansetron) to reduce serotonin-syndrome risk. Note mild platelet-mediated bleeding tendency. Do not stop antidepressants abruptly peri-operatively (discontinuation syndrome) — continue unless specifically contraindicated.

Opioid tolerance / chronic pain: continue baseline opioid (convert to IV equivalent if NBM). Expect substantially higher intra-operative and post-operative opioid requirement — titrate to effect, do not under-dose. Prioritise multimodal and regional analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID if safe, ketamine adjunct, regional block/catheter). Plan acute-on-chronic pain management and early acute pain team involvement; set realistic expectations with the patient.

Multimodal analgesia essential: combine paracetamol + NSAID/COX-2 (if no contraindication) + regional technique + opioid-sparing adjuncts (ketamine, dexamethasone, alpha-2 agonist) to minimise opioid load.

Glaucoma / raised intra-ocular pressure: avoid sustained IOP rises — smooth induction and emergence (avoid coughing/bucking/straining), consider avoiding suxamethonium (transient IOP rise) where alternatives exist, limit steep head-down positioning, ensure adequate depth before laryngoscopy. Continue topical anti-glaucoma therapy peri-operatively (note systemic effects of beta-blocker and anticholinesterase eye drops).

Continue glaucoma eye drops on the day of surgery. Be aware topical timolol can cause bradycardia/bronchospasm and topical anticholinesterases (echothiophate) prolong suxamethonium — confirm the agent.

High PONV risk (prior PONV / motion sickness): use multi-agent prophylaxis (e.g. dexamethasone at induction + ondansetron at end + consider a third agent such as a NK-1 antagonist or droperidol), prefer TIVA with propofol over volatiles, minimise opioids and avoid N₂O, ensure adequate hydration.

Migraine history: maintain hydration and avoid common triggers (prolonged fasting, hypoglycaemia, hypotension). Note interactions if the patient uses triptans/ergots. PONV-style prophylaxis is reasonable as migraineurs are prone to nausea.
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea (e.g. STOP-BANG): if positive, use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, plan extended post-op SpO₂ monitoring, have CPAP available, and use cautious sedation.

Avoid hypertensive surges (e.g. aortopathy/Marfan, raised ICP): ensure deep anaesthesia and good analgesia before stimulating events (laryngoscopy, incision, extubation), obtund the pressor response (remifentanil/esmolol/lidocaine), keep blood pressure controlled around baseline.

Pneumothorax risk (bullae / connective-tissue lung, e.g. Marfan): use lung-protective ventilation with limited peak/plateau pressures, avoid N₂O, maintain a high index of suspicion for tension pneumothorax with sudden hypoxia/hypotension/high airway pressures.

Careful positioning (joint hypermobility / fragile tissues / spinal deformity): pad pressure points generously, avoid extreme joint positions (dislocation/subluxation risk), move the anaesthetised patient slowly and with extra hands, document neurovascular status.

Bleeding/bruising tendency (e.g. vascular Ehlers-Danlos, tissue fragility): gentle airway instrumentation and line placement (vessels tear easily), check coagulation/platelets, group-and-save, consider tranexamic acid, anticipate poor haemostasis and avoid traumatic regional techniques.

Fragile tissues / difficult vascular access (connective-tissue disease): ultrasound-guided IV/arterial access, secure lines and airway devices gently (skin/tape can shear), protect eyes and pressure areas meticulously.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (e.g. cardiac amyloid): fixed low stroke volume — maintain preload, sinus rhythm and heart rate, avoid tachycardia and sudden vasodilatation, use invasive monitoring and titrated induction, beware conduction block (pacing backup) and exaggerated sensitivity to hypotension.

Autonomic dysfunction (e.g. amyloid, long-standing diabetes): expect labile blood pressure and blunted compensatory responses — invasive BP monitoring, vasopressors prepared, cautious positional changes, gastroparesis/aspiration awareness.

Difficult neuraxial access (spinal deformity / fused spine): review imaging, consider ultrasound-assisted landmarking, allow extra time, have a general-anaesthesia backup plan, and counsel the patient about higher failure/conversion rates.

Screen for pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale (severe restrictive chest disease): if suspected, obtain echocardiography, avoid hypoxia/hypercarbia/acidosis (all raise PVR), maintain RV preload and afterload carefully, and plan higher-level post-op care.

Carcinoid crisis risk: have OCTREOTIDE ready (50–100 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/h infusion; pre-treat with 100 mcg s/c 1–2 h pre-op or 50 mcg/h infusion peri-op). Treat hypotension with octreotide and vasopressin/phenylephrine — AVOID catecholamines (adrenaline/noradrenaline can paradoxically worsen vasoactive mediator release) and AVOID histamine-releasing drugs (morphine, atracurium). Invasive arterial monitoring. Avoid hypercarbia, hypothermia and light anaesthesia (all trigger mediator release).

Avoid histamine-releasing drugs (morphine, atracurium, mivacurium, large-dose rapid sux): prefer fentanyl/remifentanil, rocuronium or cisatracurium. Relevant in carcinoid, mastocytosis, phaeochromocytoma and severe atopy/anaphylaxis history.

Autonomic dysreflexia risk (spinal cord injury at/above T6): a noxious stimulus below the lesion (bladder/bowel distension, surgery) can trigger severe paroxysmal hypertension with reflex bradycardia. Ensure adequate depth even for "insensate" procedures (regional or GA — do NOT rely on the lesion for analgesia), have short-acting vasodilators ready (GTN, labetalol, phentolamine), monitor BP continuously, and remove the trigger first. Note: suxamethonium contraindicated after the acute phase (hyperkalaemia).

Peri-operative steroid cover (adrenal insufficiency / chronic steroids / hypopituitarism): give hydrocortisone at induction — minor surgery 25–50 mg, moderate 50–100 mg, major 100 mg then 50 mg q8h (or 200 mg/24h infusion) for 24–48 h, then taper to baseline. Continue usual steroids on the day of surgery. Watch for adrenal crisis (refractory hypotension) — treat with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + fluids.

Avoid NSAIDs: relevant in significant bleeding/coagulopathy, renal impairment, active peptic ulcer disease, severe asthma (aspirin-sensitive) and certain pregnancies. Use paracetamol + opioid-sparing multimodal alternatives (regional, ketamine, dexmedetomidine) instead.

Avoid mivacurium (and suxamethonium): both are metabolised by plasma cholinesterase — in cholinesterase deficiency they cause grossly prolonged paralysis. Use rocuronium (sugammadex-reversible) or cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination) instead.

Anticoagulation management: confirm agent, indication and last dose; check coagulation/anti-Xa as appropriate. Plan peri-operative interruption and bridging per thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE, AF with high CHA₂DS₂-VASc). Observe neuraxial/deep-block timing intervals (ASRA/AAGBI). Have reversal available — PCC/vitamin K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet/PCC (factor Xa inhibitors), protamine (heparin).

Inherited bleeding disorder (haemophilia / vWD): liaise with haematology for factor levels and a peri-operative replacement plan (factor VIII/IX concentrate, desmopressin for mild haemophilia A / type 1 vWD, tranexamic acid adjunct). Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs and aspirin. Confirm correction before any neuraxial/deep block.

Tracheal compression / tracheomalacia risk (large goitre, mediastinal/retrosternal mass): review CT for the level and degree of narrowing. Maintain spontaneous ventilation until the airway is secured if dynamic collapse is possible; have reinforced/longer tubes and rigid bronchoscopy / ENT backup available. Beware airway collapse on extubation — extubate awake over an airway exchange catheter, and watch for post-operative compromise.

Neck/thyroid surgery — post-operative haematoma is an airway emergency: keep clip/suture removers at the bedside, watch for swelling/stridor/voice change, and if airway compromise occurs OPEN the wound immediately to release the haematoma before re-intubation (which may be very difficult once oedema develops).

Diabetes insipidus risk (pituitary/hypothalamic surgery): monitor urine output, serum/urine osmolality and sodium closely post-op. Treat polyuria with high output + rising Na⁺ using desmopressin (DDAVP) and careful fluid replacement. Distinguish from appropriate post-operative diuresis.

Post-operative hypocalcaemia risk (total/completion thyroidectomy, parathyroid surgery): check calcium (and PTH where available) post-op; watch for perioral tingling, paraesthesia, Chvostek/Trousseau signs and (rarely) laryngospasm. Treat symptomatic or rapidly falling calcium with oral or IV calcium ± active vitamin D.

Seizure-prone procedure/patient: continue antiepileptics peri-operatively (give on the day, consider IV equivalents if NPO), avoid proconvulsant agents where relevant, and maintain normoglycaemia, normonatraemia and normocarbia.
